722.title: the birth of the cousins
722.hook: a forest sage with blazing eyes comes to a palace bedroom, a frightened widow shuts her eyes, and a son is born blind
722.howItsDone: The ancient custom in this story, called niyoga, is described in old texts and the epics; it is not practiced in Hindu families today, and the story is told for what it shows about the Kuru line.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-TWENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Last week ended with Satyavati thinking of her firstborn, and Vyasa appearing at once. Did you send someone a word? Day seven hundred twenty-two.
screen: `SHE THINKS OF HIM. HE COMES.`

segments.voice: Vyasa comes to the palace straight from the forest, and he looks it. He has lived there practicing austerities, and the text describes him: dark skin, matted hair the color of copper, a rough beard, eyes that blaze, the text says, and a smell no one would call perfume. His mother has asked him to give the house of the Kurus a son. He agrees. And he asks that they wait first. Satyavati answers: there is no time.
screen: `A SAGE FROM THE FOREST.` → `HE ASKS FOR TIME.` → `THERE IS NO TIME.`

segments.voice: This begins a new part of the serial: the birth of the cousins. Over the next days, the princes of the Kuru house come into the world: first the fathers, then the cousins who will one day face each other across a battlefield. And it starts here, with an ancient custom: when a man died without children, a learned man could be invited to father them in his name, so the line would go on. That's what Satyavati is asking. Vyasa says the widows should first keep a vow for a while, to be ready. Satyavati says the kingdom can't wait for a king. So Vyasa says: then let the princess bear my looks, my smell, my grim face. That will be her vow. Satyavati goes to the elder widow, Ambika, and tells her that a brother-in-law will come to her tonight. Ambika thinks of the heroes of the Kuru house, and waits. The lamp is lit. And in comes Vyasa, with his blazing eyes and copper hair. She's afraid, and she shuts her eyes, and keeps them shut. Afterward Vyasa tells his mother: the son will be strong and wise, a fine prince. But because his mother closed her eyes, he will be born blind. And Satyavati answers at once: a blind man can't be king of the Kurus. Give the family another. That son is Dhritarashtra. The poem lets us see how it starts: with a widow too frightened to look, a mother in a hurry, and a son who will spend his whole life near a throne he can't fully have. Vyasa ties the blindness to her closed eyes, but the text doesn't make her a villain. It shows what fear did in one night, and lets the consequences unfold.
screen: `AN OLD CUSTOM FOR A LINE.` · `NO TIME TO WAIT.` · `AMBIKA SHUTS HER EYES.` · `DHRITARASHTRA, BORN BLIND.`

Just turn toward it a little, inside, the way you'd turn toward a sound in the next room. Notice the fear, if it's there. Breathe in beside it. Breathe out, and keep your inner eyes open one moment longer. The bell holds the time.

723.title: the birth of the cousins
723.hook: the younger widow turns pale, the elder sends her maid in her place, and three very different brothers are born
723.howItsDone: Vidura's counsel to the king, the Vidura Niti in the Udyoga Parva, is read by some Hindus as a short guide to wise and honest living.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-TWENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the birth of the cousins began: Ambika shut her eyes, and Dhritarashtra was born blind. What did you look at straight on? Day seven hundred twenty-three.
screen: `A PRINCE BORN BLIND.`

segments.voice: Same palace, same sage, a different widow. Satyavati sends Vyasa to the younger princess, Ambalika. When she sees him, the blood leaves her face, and she goes pale. She doesn't shut her eyes, as her sister did. Her fear shows on her face instead. Three women, three answers to the same frightening guest, and the Kuru house is about to get its three brothers: the blind one, the pale one, and one nobody planned for at all.
screen: `A DIFFERENT WIDOW.` → `SHE GOES PALE.` → `ONE NOBODY PLANNED FOR.`

segments.voice: Vyasa tells his mother: because she turned pale, the son will be pale, and that will be his name. Pandu, the pale one. He will be a mighty prince, Vyasa says, and his own sons will be great. So now there are two heirs, one blind and one pale. And Satyavati, still not at peace, asks Vyasa for one more son from the elder widow. But Ambika can't face him again. She remembers his face and his smell, and she does something no one expected: she dresses her maid in her own ornaments, and sends her in her place. The maid isn't afraid. She rises when he enters, greets him with respect, and serves him. And Vyasa is pleased with her. He tells her: you are no longer a servant. And your son will be virtuous and wise. He then tells his mother everything: how the princess deceived him, and how the maid honored him. Then he goes back to the forest. That son is Vidura. The text later explains that he is the god of dharma himself, born as a man because of a sage's curse; that's a story for another day. So here they are, the three brothers. One can't see. One is pale. And the one born of a woman who simply showed respect, the son of a servant, will grow up to be the palace's voice of wisdom, and, because of his mother's place, the one who can never be king. This is the generation before the cousins. Their sons are the ones who will meet on the field.

724.title: the birth of the cousins
724.hook: the three brothers grow up, the pale one is crowned, and a princess of Gandhara learns her husband is blind and ties a cloth over her own eyes
724.howItsDone: In Hindu retellings Gandhari is remembered as a figure of pativrata, devotion to a husband, and the blindfold is the image tellers and painters use for her.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-TWENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in the birth of the cousins: Pandu the pale, and Vidura, the maid's son, born because she met a stranger with respect. Whom did you greet? Day seven hundred twenty-four.
screen: `THREE BROTHERS.`

segments.voice: A strip of cloth, folded over and over, tied behind the head. That's the image this part of the story leaves behind. A young princess named Gandhari, from the land of Gandhara, has been promised to a prince of the Kurus. Then she learns that he is blind. She takes a cloth, folds it, and binds her own eyes. Before we get to why, we need to see the boys grow up.
screen: `A CLOTH, FOLDED MANY TIMES.` → `A PROMISED PRINCESS.` → `SHE BINDS HER OWN EYES.`

segments.voice: With the three boys born, the text says, the land of the Kurus flourishes: rains on time, full harvests, cities busy and safe. Bhishma raises the princes as his own, and trains them. Each grows into a gift. Dhritarashtra, the text says, becomes the strongest. Pandu becomes the finest archer. And Vidura, the text says, has no equal in knowing dharma. Then comes the question of who rules. Dhritarashtra is the eldest. But he's blind, and the text says that's why he is passed over. Vidura is wise, but his mother was a servant, and so he's passed over too. The crown goes to Pandu, the younger. Hold on to that. Some readers find, in a firstborn watching his younger brother take the throne, a seed of much that follows. Now Bhishma looks for wives. He hears of Gandhari, daughter of the king of Gandhara, and asks for her for Dhritarashtra. Her family hesitates over a blind groom, then agrees. And when Gandhari hears, she binds her eyes, resolving, the text says, out of regard for her husband, never to have more than he has. Her brother, Shakuni, brings her to Hastinapura. Remember his name; he'll matter later. Readers take the blindfold more than one way. Some see a wife's complete devotion. Some see a woman refusing to be the one who sees in a marriage she didn't choose. Some see grief, worn on the face. The text gives the reason in her husband's honor, and leaves the rest of her silent. Two people who cannot see now sit beside the throne, one by birth and one by choice, and a pale king sits on it.
screen: `THE KURU LAND FLOURISHES.` · `THE CROWN GOES TO PANDU.` · `GANDHARI BINDS HER EYES.` · `SHAKUNI BRINGS HER HOME.`

The bell holds the time.

725.title: the birth of the cousins
725.hook: King Pandu, out hunting, shoots a deer that turns out to be a sage, and the dying sage's curse shuts the door on his sons
725.howItsDone: Ahimsa, not harming living beings, is an important value in Hindu traditions, and stories like Kindama's are retold to show how seriously a harm, even in a lawful hunt, can be taken.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-TWENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in the birth of the cousins: the crown went to Pandu, and Gandhari bound her eyes. What did you share with someone close? Day seven hundred twenty-five.
screen: `A PALE KING CROWNED.`

segments.voice: A stag and a doe, together in a quiet forest clearing. A king on the hunt sees them through the trees, draws his bow, and shoots, quickly, without a word of warning. The arrows strike the stag, and it falls. And then, lying in the grass, it speaks, in a man's voice. King Pandu has just shot a sage. What the dying stag says next will shape the cousins' story.
screen: `A STAG AND A DOE.` → `THE ARROWS STRIKE.` → `THE DEER SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Back up a little. Pandu has had a good reign. At her self-choice, the princess Kunti, adopted daughter of King Kuntibhoja, chose him for her husband. Bhishma also brought him a second wife, Madri, sister of the king of the Madras. Pandu rode out and won wars, and filled the treasury. Then he went to live in the forest, with both his wives, and spent his days hunting. That's where he meets the deer. The stag is a sage named Kindama, who had taken a deer's form to be with his wife. And as he dies, he says: even a king who hunts should not strike creatures in a moment like this. You've killed me in a moment of love. So hear this. When you go to your wife in love, you will die. And he dies. Pandu is undone. He grieves for the sage, and for himself. He's a king with no son, and now he can never father one. So he makes a decision: he'll give up the throne's life entirely, and live as an ascetic, begging, fasting, with no home. He gives away his jewels and royal robes to Brahmanas, and sends his attendants back to Hastinapura with the news. Kunti and Madri refuse to go back. They say they'll practice austerities beside him. Notice the turn. Yesterday, the crown went to Pandu and passed over his blind brother. Today, the crowned king sits in a forest, unable to have heirs, while back in the palace, Dhritarashtra and Gandhari remain. The story has quietly tipped. And Pandu, looking at his empty future, begins to ask how the line can go on without him.
screen: `KUNTI AND MADRI.` · `A KING GOES TO THE FOREST.` · `KINDAMA'S CURSE.` · `A KING WITH NO HEIRS.`

726.title: the birth of the cousins
726.hook: in the forest, Kunti tells Pandu about a mantra a sage gave her as a girl, and three gods are called
726.howItsDone: In Hindu tradition, Indra is praised in Vedic hymns, Vayu is the wind and the breath, and Dharma is righteousness itself; in this story they become fathers of the Pandava brothers.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-TWENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in the birth of the cousins: Pandu's arrow, Kindama's curse, and a king in the forest with no way to have sons. What did you pause before? Day seven hundred twenty-six.
screen: `A KING WITH NO HEIRS.`

segments.voice: Years before any of this, a girl named Kunti served a sage in her father's house. He was Durvasa, a sage hard to please, and she served him so carefully that, when he left, he gave her a gift: a mantra. With it, she could call any god she chose, and have a son by him. She has kept it quiet ever since. Now her husband sits in the forest, cursed, asking how his line can go on. And Kunti speaks.
screen: `A GIRL SERVES A SAGE.` → `A MANTRA, GIVEN.` → `KEPT QUIET FOR YEARS.`

segments.voice: Pandu raises it first. He tells Kunti of the old custom, the same one that brought him into the world through Vyasa, and asks her to have sons for him by a worthy man. Kunti answers with her secret: the mantra. Pandu is overjoyed. Which god first? He chooses Dharma, the god of righteousness, so the eldest son will be just. Kunti calls, and Dharma comes, and a son is born. A voice from the sky blesses the child, the text says, and he's named Yudhishthira. Then Pandu asks for a son of great strength. Kunti calls Vayu, the wind, and Bhima is born. The text tells a story to show what he is: as an infant, he tumbles from his mother's lap onto a mountain, and it's the rock that shatters. Then Pandu wants a son who'll be foremost among warriors. He keeps vows himself, and Kunti calls Indra, king of the gods. Arjuna is born, and again a voice from the sky speaks over him. Three sons: justice, strength, and skill. But notice what Kunti doesn't say. She tells Pandu about the mantra. She doesn't tell him everything about how she first learned what it could do. That piece waits for days ahead. Notice, too, that this story is shaped like the one we just finished. A line with no heir, a hidden gift from a sage, and a woman who finally speaks about it. Satyavati's secret saved the Kuru house once. Now Kunti's does the same, in the next generation. The cousins are arriving.
screen: `PANDU ASKS FOR SONS.` · `KUNTI'S MANTRA.` · `DHARMA, VAYU, INDRA.` · `WHAT KUNTI DOESN'T SAY.`

727.title: the birth of the cousins
727.hook: the cousins grow up under one roof, and a rivalry is born with them
727.howItsDone: Some Hindu families tell the Mahabharata to children a piece at a time, and the boyhood of Bhima and Duryodhana, with the poisoned meal and the serpent realm, is one of the pieces told.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-TWENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in the birth of the cousins, Kunti's mantra called Dharma, Vayu and Indra, and Yudhishthira, Bhima and Arjuna were born. Did you tell a younger person what you see growing in them? Day seven hundred twenty-seven.
screen: `JUSTICE, STRENGTH, SKILL.`

segments.voice: A fruit tree in a royal garden, and a crowd of boys up in its branches, reaching for fruit. Down below stands Bhima, the second son of Pandu. He puts his foot against the trunk and kicks. The tree shakes, and the boys come tumbling down with the fruit. In the water he grabs his cousins and holds them under until they gasp. In the dust he drags them by the hair. The Mahabharata says he meant no malice; it was a boy's play. But one of the boys on the ground is Duryodhana, the eldest son of Dhritarashtra. And he doesn't forget. Today the birth of the cousins ends with one more birth: a grudge.
screen: `A TREE FULL OF COUSINS.` → `BHIMA KICKS THE TRUNK.` → `DURYODHANA DOESN'T FORGET.`

segments.voice: The story moves quickly now. Madri, with Kunti's help, has twin sons, Nakula and Sahadeva. In Hastinapura, Gandhari's sons are born, Duryodhana the eldest. And in the forest, Pandu dies. Sages bring Kunti and the five sons of Pandu to Hastinapura, and the two families of cousins now live in one palace. They study, eat and play together. And in the text, play is where the trouble starts. Bhima is stronger than all of them, and he never lets them forget it. Duryodhana watches, and the story says jealousy takes hold of him. So he makes a plan. He arranges a day of water sports by the Ganga, with pavilions and food. Into Bhima's food goes poison. When Bhima, worn out and heavy, lies down by the river, Duryodhana binds him and pushes him into the water. Bhima sinks, down and down, into the realm of the Nagas, the serpent people. The snakes bite him, and in the story their venom works against the poison. The Naga king receives him, and Bhima is given a drink that makes him stronger still. Back in Hastinapura, the brothers come home without him. Kunti is frantic, and she says aloud what she suspects. Vidura, the wise uncle, tells her to keep quiet: if she accuses Duryodhana openly, he may turn on her other sons. Then Bhima walks home, alive and stronger, and tells his brothers everything. Yudhishthira's answer is to say nothing for now, and to guard one another. So that's where these six days of births leave us. The cousins were born in one family. Now something else has been born between them, and the brothers have learned to keep their eyes open.

Remember one small moment between you, a game, a fight, a shared meal. Don't judge who was right. Just let the memory come, and hold it lightly. If an old sting is still there, notice where it sits. If there's warmth, let it stay a while. The bell holds the time.

728.title: Karna's abandonment
728.hook: a girl in a king's house is given a mantra by a sage, and tries it on the sun
728.howItsDone: Some Hindus greet the rising sun with folded hands or an offering of water, honoring Surya, the god Pritha called with Durvasa's mantra.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-TWENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the birth of the cousins: rough play, a poisoned meal, and a grudge that started young. Did any small resentment show up, and did you name it? Day seven hundred twenty-eight.
screen: `A GRUDGE IS BORN TOO.`

segments.voice: Two days ago, Kunti told Pandu about a sage's mantra, and held one piece back. Today the poem steps back in time and tells that piece. Before Kunti was a queen, she was a girl called Pritha, raised in the house of a king named Kuntibhoja. When the sage Durvasa came as a guest, the hard work of looking after him fell to her, and she did it well. His gift was the mantra. And now she is young, unmarried, alone with words that can summon a god. Today Karna's abandonment begins, with a girl wondering whether the words really work.
screen: `PRITHA, IN KUNTIBHOJA'S HOUSE.` → `DURVASA'S GIFT.` → `DO THE WORDS WORK?`

segments.voice: With Durvasa's mantra, he told her, she could call any god she liked, and that god would come to her and give her a son. Then he left. And the text says that, out of curiosity, she tries it. She looks up at the sun rising, and she speaks the mantra. And Surya, the sun god, comes. Here the story slows down, because Pritha is frightened. She tells him she only wanted to see if the gift worked. She's a girl in her father's house. She asks him to go. And Surya answers that a god called by this mantra can't return for nothing. A son will be born. But he promises her something too: that she'll remain a maiden afterward, her honor kept. So on the week's last day, the story hands us a new beginning, older than all the others. Before the five brothers, before the cousins, Kunti had a son. Nobody in the palace knows it. Notice how human the scene is. There's no villain in it. There's a sage's gift, a girl's curiosity, a god who keeps the rules of the mantra, and fear. And out of that fear, over the next few days, will come a choice that echoes through the whole poem.
screen: `A SAGE'S GIFT: A MANTRA.` · `SHE TRIES IT ON THE SUN.` · `SURYA COMES, AND SHE IS AFRAID.` · `A SON BEFORE ALL THE OTHERS.` · then, large: `NOBODY IN THE PALACE KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes, and a week to look back on. Let the breath slow down. Bring to mind one thing you started this week, maybe a little out of curiosity, the way Pritha tried those words. A conversation, a habit, a question. Don't decide yet whether it was wise. Just look at it, and see where it might lead. If you'd like, rest your attention on the morning light, wherever it fell for you today. The bell holds the time.
